item.research_question: How do crystal orientation, temperature, and strain rate influence the mechanical properties and plastic deformation mechanisms of an equiatomic FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy?
item.processing_route: Molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS software with Embedded-atom method (EAM) potential; model size 108.3 Å × 108.3 Å × 180.5 Å (180,000 atoms); relaxation via conjugate gradient and NVT ensemble (Nose–Hoover thermostat) with heating to 1000 K and cooling to 300 K; tensile loading at orientations <110>, <1-12>, <-111>; temperatures 10 K, 300 K, 600 K; strain rates 10^8 s⁻¹, 10^9 s⁻¹, 10^10 s⁻¹
item.test_conditions: Uniaxial tensile loading; temperatures: 10 K, 300 K, 600 K; strain rates: 10^8 s⁻¹, 10^9 s⁻¹, 10^10 s⁻¹; crystal orientations: <110>, <1-12>, <-111>; time step 1 fs; periodic boundary conditions
key_findings: The <-111> direction exhibited the highest elastic modulus and yield strength due to atomic close-packing along (111) planes.
Yield strength and yield strain decreased significantly as temperature increased from 10 K to 600 K.
Dislocation density decreased with increasing temperature due to enhanced atomic mobility and dislocation annihilation.
Yield strength was relatively insensitive to strain rate variations (10^8 to 10^10 s⁻¹) within the tested range.
Higher strain rates resulted in higher dislocation densities and elevated flow stress after yielding.
Plastic deformation was primarily mediated by Shockley partial dislocations (1/6<112>) and stair-rod immobile dislocations (1/6<110>), forming intrinsic and extrinsic stacking faults.
No FCC-to-BCC phase transformation was observed; HCP atoms were attributed to stacking faults rather than a true phase change.
Vacancy aggregation played a critical role in dislocation nucleation, with dislocations predominantly forming at vacancy sites.
item.mechanism: The authors explain that elevated temperatures intensify atomic thermal vibrations, weakening bonding forces and lowering the critical resolved shear stress, which facilitates dislocation nucleation and motion, thereby reducing yield strength. Conversely, higher strain rates do not significantly affect yield strength but increase flow stress because the rapid deformation prevents dislocations from annihilating or rearranging, leading to higher dislocation accumulation and internal resistance. Anisotropy arises from differences in atomic packing density and bonding strength along different crystallographic directions, with the <-111> direction requiring higher stress to initiate plastic deformation due to alignment with close-packed planes.
item.limitations: The study was conducted at the nanoscale with relatively small variations in strain rates, which may limit the generalizability of the strain rate insensitivity finding. Additionally, no significant deformation twins were observed, likely due to high twinning nucleation energy under the simulated conditions, whereas experimental studies have reported annealing twins in similar alloys.
item.future_work: The authors state they are currently conducting related experiments to explore twinning behavior during annealing and plan to compare preliminary experimental results with simulation findings to distinguish between deformation twins and annealing twins in terms of formation conditions and mechanisms.
quotes: The results revealed that the FeNiCrMn HEA exhibited significant anisotropy under loading along different orientations, with the maximum yield stress observed along the <11-1> direction.
Elevated temperatures intensify atomic thermal vibrations, making it easier for atoms to deviate from their equilibrium positions and facilitating dislocation nucleation and movement.
Higher strain rates correspond to instantaneous dislocation density strengthening, which leads to higher flow stress.
